paper.title: Development and External Validation of an Interpretable Machine Learning Model for Predicting Positive Surgical Margin After Robot-Assisted Radical Prostatectomy.
paper.abstract:
Purpose: To develop an interpretable, externally validated machine learning (ML) model for predicting positive surgical margin (PSM) after robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) using routine preoperative variables.
Patients And Methods: We retrospectively analyzed patients who underwent RARP at two Chinese medical centers. The primary cohort included 369 patients and was divided into a training set (n = 258) and an internal validation set (n = 111) using a stratified sampling strategy, while an independent external cohort of 243 patients was used for external validation. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was applied for feature selection. Six ML models were trained in the training set and compared in both the internal and external validation sets. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, Brier score, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis was used to interpret the final model, and a web-based calculator was developed for individualized prediction.
Results: Among the six ML models, Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) achieved robust discrimination with an AUC of 0.9095 in the training set and 0.8669 in the internal validation set. The model maintained good performance in the external validation set (AUC 0.8281). The LightGBM model also showed acceptable calibration, the lowest Brier scores, and favorable net benefit. SHAP analysis identified clinical T stage, PSA density, lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio, prostate volume, positive core rate, perineural invasion, and biopsy Gleason Grade Group as the main contributors to model prediction.
Conclusion: The LightGBM model demonstrated favorable discrimination and calibration for predicting PSM after RARP. The SHAP-based interpretation and web-based calculator may facilitate individualized preoperative risk assessment; however, prospective validation in broader multicenter populations is required before routine clinical implementation.

paper.title: Prediction of long-term mortality in maintenance hemodialysis patients using machine learning survival models: a prospective multicenter study with SHAP-based interpretation.
paper.abstract:
Background: Accurate and interpretable prediction of long-term mortality in maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) patients remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and externally validate machine learning survival models integrating clinical, nutritional, inflammatory, and anthropometric predictors.
Methods: This prospective multicenter cohort included 1,129 MHD patients from eight dialysis centers in China. Patients were allocated to training (n = 645), internal validation (n = 274), and independent external test (n = 210) cohorts. Predictors were selected using LASSO-Cox regression and Survival Boruta. Five survival machine learning models were developed and evaluated for discrimination, prediction error, calibration, and clinical utility. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to interpret model predictions.
Results: During a median follow-up of 4.53 years, 603 patients died. 14 predictors were selected for model development. In the external test cohort, gradient boosting survival analysis (GBS) achieved a C-index of 0.748 (95% CI, 0.705-0.790), a 5-year time-dependent AUC of 0.799 (95% CI, 0.726-0.861) and the lowest integrated Brier score (0.141) among the five models. GBS also demonstrated reasonable calibration, although its discrimination was not significantly superior to that of random survival forest. SHAP analysis identified age, prealbumin and diabetes mellitus as the leading contributors to model predictions.
Conclusion: An interpretable GBS model integrating routinely available clinical, nutritional, inflammatory, and anthropometric predictors demonstrated promising performance for long-term mortality risk stratification in MHD patients. Further external validation and prospective clinical evaluation are warranted.

paper.title: Training AI Models for Automatic Segmentation and Quantification of White Matter Lesions Across Multiple Centres.
paper.abstract: Background and Objectives: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are MRI biomarkers associated with vascular, neurodegenerative, and mixed neurological diseases. Manual WMH segmentation and volume quantification are time-consuming and operator-dependent, making artificial intelligence (AI) an attractive alternative. This study examined how WMH segmentation and volume-quantification performance changed across nested training cohorts with joint increases in participant and annotated-lesion counts. Materials and Methods: More than 18,000 WMH lesions were manually annotated by four expert raters from multicentre 3T FLAIR ADNI patient studies (n = 300: HC = 108, MCI = 108, and AD = 84) (age: 71.44 ± 7.50; education: 16.10 ± 2.37 years; 142 males). Three nnU-Net models were trained on different numbers of annotated lesions (18,034, 11,496, and 4685 lesions). Models' performance was evaluated using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) with 5-fold cross-validation. We evaluated generalisability on an independent external dataset of n = 62 patients from European and Asian centres using quantitative and qualitative analyses via a neuroradiological 4-point visual rating scale completed by two expert raters. Results: DSC increased with training set size in both the cross-validation datasets (0.64 ± 0.03, 0.68 ± 0.04, and 0.70 ± 0.02) and the external dataset (0.67, 0.73, and 0.75), with statistically significant improvements and good-to-excellent expert-rated segmentation quality (mean score: 3.23). The model trained on 18,034 lesions achieved performance within the range reported for currently available medical devices. Conclusions: Increasing both the number of participants and annotated WMH lesions substantially improves AI-based WMH segmentation and quantification. Training on more than 18,000 lesions produced robust generalisation, expert-rated good-to-excellent segmentation quality, and performance within the range reported for currently available medical devices.

paper.title: Dual-Magnification Deep Learning Predicts KRASG12D Status from H&E Images of Pancreatic Cancer: A Multi-Cohort Study.
paper.abstract: Background: KRAS mutations occur in over 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDAC), and KRASG12D is the most frequent variant. G12D-selective inhibitors are now in clinical development, but computational pathology has so far predicted mutation status only at the gene level, leaving allele-specific prediction unexplored. Because genomic testing can be time-consuming and costly, a tool that predicts KRASG12D mutation status from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images could help identify patients for confirmatory molecular testing and potential treatment with KRASG12D inhibitors. Here we present a multi-scale framework that predicts KRASG12D status from H&E whole-slide images, with integration of computed tomography (CT). Methods: Two public cohorts (TCGA, CPTAC) formed the training set, and an independent external cohort (Osaka Metropolitan University Hospital) served as validation. We developed a dual-magnification pipeline. In the high-magnification branch, a pathology foundation model (CONCH v1.5) was fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and an attention-based multiple-instance learning head on 20× patches; in the low-magnification branch, a generative image model encoded a whole-slide overview. The two branches were integrated by late fusion into a multi-scale pathomics model, which was further combined with a radiomics model of CT. Results: The multi-scale pathomics model reached a pooled internal test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.611 and an external AUC of 0.701. In the external patients with CT, the combined model reached an AUC of 0.772, compared with 0.753 for pathomics alone. Conclusions: KRASG12D status leaves a signal in routine H&E images and CT of PDAC that deep learning can detect and that transfers to an independent institution. After prospective validation, the framework might help prioritize patients for KRAS testing.

paper.title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Pretrained Multi-Label Chest X-Ray Classifiers: A Retrospective External Validation of Seven Models.
paper.abstract: Background/Objectives: Chest radiograph classifiers are usually benchmarked within their training distribution, whereas deployment exposes them to new populations, equipment, and labeling conventions. This study quantified out-of-distribution (OOD) performance of seven public pretrained classifiers. Methods: Six DenseNet-121 models and one ResNet-50 TorchXRayVision model were evaluated without fine-tuning on 18,424 Brazilian BRAX studies for seven common labels. The in-distribution (ID) performances of the three models trained on ChestX-ray14 were measured on held-out patients. Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) were compared with a paired patient-level bootstrap; calibration, operating points, and subgroups were assessed. Results: OOD macro AUROC was 0.733-0.741 for three models trained with PadChest and 0.652-0.677 for four single-source models (all between-group differences significant). Relative to held-out ID performance, macro AUROC decreased by 6.0-11.4 percentage points. Expected calibration error of default outputs (0.028-0.392) largely reflected score normalization and fell to 0.001-0.003 after recalibration; sensitivity at default operating points was 0.035-0.797. Macro AUROC was lower for anteroposterior than posteroanterior radiographs (0.499-0.605 vs. 0.691-0.796), also within age groups; residual confounding remains possible. Conclusions: In this single Brazilian cohort, ID benchmarks overestimated external performance, and default outputs and operating points did not transfer. Local validation, recalibration, and subgroup-stratified reporting are needed before clinical use.

paper.title: Do Severity Prediction Models for Paediatric Appendicitis Work in Another Hospital? A Bidirectional External Validation and Local Recalibration Study.
paper.abstract: Background/Objectives: Models predicting complicated appendicitis in children could support selection for non-operative management, but are rarely validated in a second hospital. We examined how severity models transport between hospitals, why they fail and what local recalibration can achieve. Methods: Using two open paediatric cohorts, we developed models in Regensburg (164 operated children with histology-verified appendicitis, 50 complicated) and validated them in Düsseldorf (229 operated children, 49 complicated), and vice versa. Laboratory, clinical and ultrasound models, random forest, XGBoost and two clinical scores were compared. We examined heterogeneity in case mix, predictor measurement, documentation and outcome definition, and local updating with 25-150 patients. Results: Internal AUCs of 0.81-0.82 fell to 0.71-0.74 externally; calibration slopes were 0.52-0.70 and risks were overestimated (observed/expected 0.61-0.85), whereas the reverse direction underestimated risk (1.40-1.62). The hospitals differed in age range, referral and management pathways, documentation practices and the histological definition of complicated appendicitis. A larger same-hospital development sample did not improve calibration. Recalibration with 50 local patients (11 events) brought the median calibration slope close to 1, but estimates were imprecise; precise estimation would require several hundred events. Including non-operatively managed children without histology inflated internal AUC from 0.82 to 0.88. Conclusions: In operated children, discrimination was partly preserved between hospitals, but calibration was not. Because outcome definitions, patient selection and documentation differed, poor transportability cannot be attributed to the models alone; the comparability of clinical data and outcomes should be established before models are transferred or recalibrated.

paper.title: Attention-Based Dual-Branch Deep Learning for Overall Survival Prediction in Patients with Brain Metastases Using MRI: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
paper.abstract: Objectives: To develop and validate an attention-based deep learning (DL) model to predict overall survival (OS) in patients with brain metastases (BM) using pre-treatment magnetic resonance image (MRI). Methods: A total of 216 BM patients treated with radiotherapy or neurosurgical resection were retrospectively enrolled from two hospitals and divided into training (n = 128), internal validation (n = 56), and external validation (n = 32) cohorts. Three feature aggregation methods and seven radiomics models were developed to predict OS. A DL model named DeepBMSurv, incorporating a cross-attention mechanism, was built using pre-treatment MR images. Its prognostic performance was compared with radiomics models and graded prognostic assessment (GPA). A nomogram integrating GPA, radiomics score (Rad-score) and DL score (DL_RiskScore) was also developed. Model performance was assessed by the concordance index (C-index). Results: Among the radiomics models, the RadScoremean model showed the most stable discrimination across cohorts, with C-index values of 0.685, 0.672, and 0.671 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts. DeepBMSurv achieved numerically higher C-indices than both the radiomics model and GPA model, with C-indices of 0.806 vs. 0.685 vs. 0.620 in the training cohort, 0.755 vs. 0.672 vs. 0.628 in the internal validation cohort, and 0.733 vs. 0.671 vs. 0.579 in the external validation cohort. The nomogram integrating DL_RiskScore, Rad-score, and GPA achieved C-index values of 0.809, 0.764 and 0.733 in training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. Conclusions: A DL model based on pre-treatment MRI can effectively predict survival outcomes in patients with BM, offering a potential tool for individualized prognostic risk stratification.

paper.title: A Deep-Learning-Derived Ultrasound Framework for Hepatic Steatosis Detection and Integrated Fibrosis Assessment: A Multicenter Study.
paper.abstract: Background/Objectives: We aimed to develop an integrated B-mode ultrasound framework for hepatic steatosis detection and fibrosis assessment in patients with suspected metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Methods: This multicenter study prospectively included 734 participants with 2485 ultrasound images from eight centers (April 2023-November 2025). A Global Attention Mechanism-enhanced Cross-Attention Multi-Scale Vision Transformer was used to derive a steatosis signature in Dataset A (Centers 1-3, n = 245), with external testing in Datasets B (Centers 4-5, n = 294) and C (Centers 6-8, n = 195). The signature was then integrated with liver elasticity and clinical and laboratory variables to develop a fibrosis prediction model in Dataset B, with external testing in Dataset C. Results: The steatosis signature achieved AUROCs of 0.887 (95% CI, 0.831-0.938) and 0.968 (95% CI, 0.932-0.994) in Datasets B and C, respectively, significantly outperforming the hepatic steatosis index, fatty liver index, and the junior radiologist (AUROC range: 0.728-0.794; all p < 0.05), while performing comparably to the senior radiologist (AUROC range: 0.864-0.932). The fibrosis model achieved an AUROC of 0.849 (95% CI, 0.762-0.916) in Dataset C and significantly outperformed elasticity, fibrosis-4 index, aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease fibrosis score (AUROC range: 0.431-0.697; all p < 0.05). For F0 versus F1, the model also achieved an AUROC of 0.841 (95% CI, 0.745-0.922), significantly outperforming all comparators (all p < 0.05). Conclusions: This integrated framework provides a noninvasive approach for steatosis case-finding and early fibrosis risk stratification in patients with suspected MASLD.

paper.title: Machine Learning and Delta Habitat Radiomics Predict Neoadjuvant Chemoradiotherapy Response in Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: A Multicenter Study.
paper.abstract: Background: Accurate and non-invasive prediction of response to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (NCRT) and long-term outcomes in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) remains challenging. This multicenter study developed and validated machine-learning (ML) classifiers based on delta habitat magnetic-resonance image (MRI) radiomics to address this unmet need. Materials and Methods: A total of 1228 LARC patients who completed NCRT across five tertiary centers were retrospectively divided into four independent datasets. Serial T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images (DWI) acquired before and after NCRT were co-registered, and delta habitat radiomic features were extracted. Fourteen ML algorithms were trained and externally validated for three signature sets: T2 delta habitat, DWI delta habitat, and combined delta habitat. Model performance was assessed with ROC analysis, Kaplan-Meier survival curves, and decision-curve analysis (DCA). Results: Among the 14 classifier configurations evaluated, the combined T2WI+DWI delta habitat multilayer perceptron (MLP) model achieved AUCs of 0.932, 0.903, 0.925, and 0.922 in the training, validation, Test1, and Test2 cohorts, respectively. The corresponding AUCs for the T2 delta habitat model were 0.801, 0.813, 0.867, and 0.788, whereas those for the DWI delta habitat model were 0.831, 0.769, 0.895, and 0.832 for predicting NCRT response. The combined delta habitat signature provided risk stratification for disease-free and overall survival. Importantly, the combined delta habitat model also discriminated postoperative pathological categories (ypT1N0M0 and ypCR) in an exploratory analysis. Conclusions: Delta habitat MRI radiomics showed potential for predicting NCRT response in patients with LARC. Associations with survival and discrimination of postoperative pathological categories were exploratory and require further validation. The MLP-based combined delta habitat model shows promise for clinical translation.

paper.title: A radiomics-based interpretable model to predict post-cystectomy disease-free survival in muscle invasive bladder cancer: a multicenter retrospective cohort study.
paper.abstract:
Objective: To develop and validate an interpretable machine learning (ML) model based on CT radiomics to predict the 2-year disease-free survival (DFS) in muscle invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) patients with multicenter validation.
Methods: A total of 377 patients with MIBC who underwent radical cystectomy were included from five institutions between November 2012 and February 2022. Of these, 264 patients were assigned to the training set, and 113 to the test set. The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used to select radiomics features and construct radiomics score (Rad-score). Five common ML models were developed by combining the Rad-score with significant clinicopathologic factors. The shapley additive explanation (SHAP) method was employed to visualize the prediction process.
Results: The Rad-score was constructed by eleven radiomics features, achieving AUCs of 0.827 and 0.771 in predicting 2-year DFS in the training and test sets, respectively. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed significant differences in DFS between the high-risk and low-risk groups stratified by the Rad-score in both the training (hazard ratio: 5.40[95%CI: 3.89-7.49]) and test sets (hazard ratio: 6.11[95%CI: 3.39-11.02]). When combined with Rad-score, pT stage, variant histology, tumor size, and age, the RF model achieved the best performance, with AUCs of 0.924 and 0.850 in the training and test sets, respectively. SHAP analysis indicated that Rad-score and pT stage contributed the most to the RF model's predictions.
Conclusions: The proposed ML model demonstrated the potential to accurately predict early recurrence and mortality in MIBC patients, aiding personalized treatment decision-making.

paper.title: Decision fusion model for predicting WHO/ISUP grade of clear cell renal cell carcinoma based on multi-phase CT radiomics: a multicenter study.
paper.abstract:
Background: The pathological grading of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) plays a critical role in both its diagnosis and treatment. This study aimed to develop a decision fusion model based on multi-phase CT to predict the WHO/ISUP grade of ccRCC.
Methods: This retrospective study included clinical and radiological data from patients with ccRCC from three centers. Radiomics features from both the arterial phase and venous phase of CT images were extracted. After feature dimensionality reduction and selection, optimized features from the arterial phase, venous phase, and their combination were input into six machine learning classifiers to construct 18 radiomics models. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to select the optimal radiomics model. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression was applied to select clinical-radiological features and establish a clinical model. A combined model then was developed using stacking ensemble learning to integrate radiomics and clinical model. The performance of the models was evaluated using ROC curves, and the clinical utility of the models was assessed using decision curve analysis (DCA).
Results: A total of 884 ccRCC patients were ultimately included in the study (training set: n = 459; internal validation set: n = 198; external validation set: n = 227). The ExtraTrees model from the CTA_CTV group demonstrated the best performance, achieving an AUC of 0.691 in the external validation set. Subsequently, ExtraTrees classifier was used to construct the clinical model. By integrating the clinical and radiomics models using LightGBM, the combined model exhibited superior performance in the external validation cohort, with an AUC value of 0.703 (95% CI: 0.628-0.778). The combined model outperformed the clinical and radiomics models. DCA revealed that the combined model provided the highest clinical net benefit for pathological grading prediction.
Conclusion: The combined model showed potential for preoperative WHO/ISUP grading of ccRCC and may provide complementary non-invasive information for risk stratification.

paper.title: Clinicians vs. artificial intelligence in patient outcome prediction in the intensive care unit.
paper.abstract: Accurate prediction of patient outcomes in the intensive care unit (ICU) is critical for clinical decision-making. While artificial intelligence (AI) has shown potential in retrospective prediction, direct comparisons with human clinicians, particularly in prospective real-world settings, remain unclear. We conducted a mixed retrospective and prospective study to compare clinician and AI performances in ICU patient outcome prediction. In the retrospective setting, both clinicians and AI, trained on 46,631 ICU admissions, predicted 990 ICU admissions only based on patient data. In the prospective setting, clinician predictions for 238 ICU admissions were collected during active patient care, whereas AI made predictions for the same admissions using extracted patient data. Target outcomes were in-hospital and 30-day mortality, acute kidney injury, delirium, and ICU and hospital lengths of stay. In the retrospective setting, AI generally outperformed clinicians, but aggregated predictions from seven clinicians outperformed AI. In the prospective setting, subspecialized physicians generally outperformed AI, whereas physicians in training and nurses generally underperformed AI. Combinations of clinician and AI predictions often resulted in the best prediction performance. Our findings provide a comprehensive evaluation of clinician and AI performances in ICU outcome prediction under both retrospective and real-world prospective conditions, setting important prediction performance benchmarks.

paper.title: Automated limb motor assessment in Parkinson's disease via a time-frequency state-space model.
paper.abstract: Assessment of limb motor function is central to the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS), but current practice relies on subjective visual inspection. Existing deep learning approaches remain limited in characterizing the non-stationary and nonlinear dynamics of pathological extremity movement, including bradykinesia and intermittent tremor. We developed TF-Mamba, a time-frequency dynamics-aware framework for automated and standardized scoring of finger tapping, hand movements, and leg agility based on expert-consensus MDS-UPDRS ratings. The framework integrates a spatiotemporal feature backbone with a physical signal dynamics module that decomposes nonlinear joint trajectories in the time-frequency domain. The model was trained using data from 1479 patients with Parkinson's disease at four Chinese centers and independently validated in 450 patients from three centers. For five-level severity scoring, TF-Mamba achieved an AUC of up to 0.90 in external validation and outperformed state-of-the-art baselines by 8-10%. Energy Entropy, Amplitude Coefficient of Variation, and Frequency Stability were associated with clinical severity (all p < 0.001). In a reader study, the model reduced evaluation time by 60-70% and improved the agreement of junior physicians' ratings with expert consensus. Collectively, TF-Mamba provides an interpretable and scalable framework for MDS-UPDRS limb motor assessment.

paper.title: End-to-end deep learning-based electrocardiographic analysis for the detection of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
paper.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) shows heterogeneous clinical features and often leads to underdiagnosis and misdiagnosis, particularly when distinguishing it from other causes of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and among HCM subtypes. Although electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available and sensitive, limited specificity constrains its standalone diagnostic value in HCM. We developed a deep learning-based model using standard 12-lead ECGs to simultaneously screen for LVH, distinguish HCM from phenocopies, and classify major HCM subtypes. This study innovatively emulates the clinical diagnostic workflow by establishing an end-to-end, hierarchical intelligent framework that encompasses the complete diagnostic pathway, integrating three key clinical decision-making stages into a unified model. Trained on 12,618 ECGs from 11,290 patients across three centers, the model showed strong performance in the internal testing set [AUROCs for each stage: 0.97 (0.96-0.98), 0.93 (0.89-0.96), and 0.85 (0.76-0.92)] and maintained consistent performance in two independent external testing sets (FAHGMU cohort: AUROCs for each stage were 0.94, 0.87, and 0.89; FAHXMU cohort: AUROCs for each stage were 0.92, 0.80, and 0.83). Saliency analysis indicated that predictions relied on physiologically relevant ECG regions. This interpretable, ECG-based approach may support scalable HCM stratification and early phenotyping across diverse clinical settings.

paper.title: Acute illness severity index for severe cardiovascular disease patients using machine learning approaches.
paper.abstract:
Background: Common intensive care severity scores may be less accurate for critically ill patients with cardiovascular disease. We develop and validate a data-driven severity index for 30 day mortality prediction using routinely collected hospital data.
Methods: We performed a retrospective multicenter cohort study. Model development used the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care databases (39,458 admissions), split into training (10,457) and internal validation (29,001). External validation used a large United States multicenter intensive care database (9,222) and an independent Guangdong Second Provincial General Hospital cohort (235). We compared machine learning models with three established severity scores. We evaluated discrimination, calibration, clinical utility, and model explanations.
Results: Here we show that a gradient boosted decision tree model achieves the highest discrimination, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.853, 0.802, and 0.853 in the internal and two external cohorts, versus 0.724 to 0.765 for established scores. Calibration is good (standardized mortality ratio 1.00; 95% confidence interval 0.98 to 1.02) and remains consistent across age, sex, and race subgroups. Decision curve analysis shows a higher net benefit than conventional scores across thresholds of 0.20 to 0.60. Key contributors include comorbidity burden, urine output, activity status, respiratory rate, and minimum oxygen saturation.
Conclusions: A gradient boosted decision tree-based severity index improves discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility compared with conventional intensive care scores and generalizes across external cohorts. The model explanations support interpretable risk stratification for critically ill cardiovascular disease.

paper.title: A Study in Contrasts: A Head-to-Head Comparison of MRI Contrast Phases for Deep Learning Liver Segmentation.
paper.abstract:
Rationale And Objectives: This study aimed to systematically evaluate the optimal MRI contrast phase(s) for automated liver segmentation using single-phase and multiphase deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) employing both early- and late-fusion techniques.
Materials And Methods: This retrospective study included 586 hepatocellular carcinoma patients with multi-phasic contrast-enhanced MRI from an institutional database. DCNNs were trained using identical 3D U-Net-derived architectures on single phases and all possible multi-phasic combinations, with early- and late-fusion techniques, resulting in a total of 26 models. The dataset was randomly split into 70/15/15% for training/validation/testing, and performance was quantified by the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). From a collaborating site, 16 scans were used for external testing. The public LiverHccSeg dataset (n = 17) was used for additional testing. Furthermore, co-registered multiphasic examinations from the public Duke Liver Dataset (DLDS) were used as a third external test set (n = 68). Friedman's test with Dunn-Bonferroni post-hoc tests were used to compare performance across models. The top-performing model of each fusion strategy was defined by the highest Friedman mean rank.
Results: The late-fusion DCNN combining arterial, portal-venous, and delayed-phase MRI achieved superior performance across all models in the internal test set (mean DSC: 0.971 ± 0.021, P <.001 for all pairwise comparisons). The best single-phase DCNN used portal-venous phase (mean DSC: 0.970 ± 0.017) and significantly outperformed the best early-fusion DCNN based on a combination of portal-venous-, and delayed phase (mean DSC: 0.966 ± 0.036) (P < .001). The developed DCNNs demonstrated generalizable performance to external data (late-fusion: 0.961 ± 0.014, early-fusion: 0.964 ± 0.009, single-phase: 0.956 ± 0.035), the public LiverHccSeg (late-fusion: 0.911 ± 0.070, early-fusion: 0.898 ± 0.112, single-phase: 0.889 ± 0.109), and DLDS data (late-fusion: 0.907 ± 0.120, early-fusion: 0.873 ± 0.200, single-phase: 0.898 ± 0.134).
Conclusion: Optimal deep learning liver segmentation performance was achieved through late-fusion of arterial, portal-venous, and delayed-phase MRI and demonstrated generalizable performance to external data. Single-phase segmentation on portal-venous phase remained a computationally efficient alternative with satisfactory performance. The numerical gain from multiphase late fusion was small in terms of mean DSC and was most apparent as reduced variability and improved worst-case performance on external data.

paper.title: A CTA-Based model integrating the rim sign and quantitative plaque features for identification of carotid intraplaque hemorrhage.
paper.abstract:
Background: Accurate identification of carotid intraplaque hemorrhage (IPH), a key marker of plaque vulnerability, remains challenging on computed tomography angiography (CTA). We aimed to identify CTA-derived features associated with IPH and develop a CTA-based diagnostic model using high-resolution vessel wall imaging (HR-VWI) as the reference standard.
Methods: In this multicenter retrospective study, 469 patients with 1,196 carotid plaques who underwent CTA and HR-VWI within 1 month were enrolled. IPH was defined on HR-VWI. Qualitative CTA features, including the rim sign, and quantitative plaque characteristics derived from artificial intelligence-assisted CTA analysis were assessed. Independent predictors of IPH were identified using multivariable logistic regression. A diagnostic model was developed in a training cohort, and validated internally and externally.
Results: IPH was present in 277 of 1,196 plaques (23.2 %). The rim sign (OR, 13.7; 95 % CI, 6.4-29.4), fibro-lipid volume (OR, 1.5; 95 % CI, 1.2-2), and luminal stenosis (OR, 2.2; 95 % CI, 1.6-2.9) were independently associated with IPH (all P < 0.001). Luminal stenosis and fibro-lipid volume showed the highest discriminative performance (AUCs, 0.741 and 0.735), while the rim sign demonstrated high specificity (97.9 %). The combined CTA model achieved AUCs of 0.794, 0.829, and 0.803 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively.
Conclusions: The rim sign, fibro-lipid volume, and luminal stenosis are independent CTA predictors of carotid IPH. Integrating qualitative CTA markers with AI-derived quantitative plaque features enables accurate, noninvasive identification of IPH and may improve CTA-based assessment of carotid plaque vulnerability.

paper.title: Biological augmentation of electronic health records through estimation of patient proteomes.
paper.abstract: High-dimensional proteomic profiling can improve clinical risk prediction and provide insight into disease biology, but routine acquisition of omic data at population scale remains impractical. We developed Real-world AI-based Biomarker Inference Technology (RABIT), a machine learning framework that biologically augments electronic health records (EHRs) by projecting longitudinal clinical histories into a high-dimensional proteomic representation space learned from paired EHR and plasma proteomics. RABIT was trained using patients with paired EHRs and measured plasma proteomics and externally validated in an independent cohort with paired data. RABIT profiles showed broad concordance with measured protein expression and more closely resembled measured proteomics than their input EHR. Incorporating these biologically augmented representations improved 5-year disease onset prediction across 14 conditions (n = 449,223; mean adjusted AUPRC increase of 33.7%) and generalized to an external cohort (n = 1,038,419; mean adjusted AUPRC increase of 70.3%). RABIT profiles reproduced clinically meaningful organ-specific biological changes in response to aging and further outperformed models built from comprehensive established clinical predictors in prediction of chronic kidney disease progression, major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and response to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer. Last, RABIT enabled biological signatures derived from small discovery cohorts to be extended to population-scale clinical datasets, generating clinically relevant hypotheses linking cytomegalovirus-associated immune states to variation in brain tumor outcomes. Together, these results demonstrate that biological augmentation of EHRs can enable molecularly informed clinical prediction and hypothesis generation at population scale.

paper.title: Localisation and classification of preselected thyroid ultrasound nodules: cross-cohort performance of a public-dataset model with limited local data.
paper.abstract: Public-dataset models are rarely characterised on local data. A YOLOv8m model trained on the fine-needle-aspiration-labelled public TN5000 thyroid ultrasound dataset was tested on two independent cohorts. Images were cropped to a preselected nodule. Mean average precision at intersection-over-union 0.5 (mAP@0.5) fell from 0.825 on TN5000 to 0.415 on the Stanford Artificial Intelligence in Medicine and Imaging (AIMI) cohort and 0.420 on the institutional cohort, indicating domain shift. Stepwise fine-tuning raised institutional mAP@0.5 to 0.630 (95% confidence interval, CI, 0.525-0.730) but degraded TN5000 performance to 0.323-0.421, indicating catastrophic forgetting; single-stage mixed retraining reached 0.611 (0.521-0.716) and 0.788-0.819 on TN5000 up to a 40% institutional proportion. Training each selected configuration three times gave standard deviations of 0.057 and 0.069, larger than any difference between adjacent fine-tuning sizes, and neither repeat of the 30% mixed model was separable from the baseline, so no configuration is identified as best. After multiplicity correction the only separable adjacent step was a decline, from 40% to 50% institutional data. Lesion-level detection exceeded 0.90 sensitivity at about one false positive per imaging study, but discrimination of the cytology-defined malignant class was weak (end-to-end area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.701, 95% CI 0.610-0.780), and its gain over the baseline did not survive multiplicity correction (adjusted p = 0.059). Positive predictive value was 0.19 to 0.24 at 10% prevalence. Under the training design evaluated, mixed public-plus-local training retained source-domain performance better than fine-tuning; these retrospective, exploratory findings do not establish clinical readiness.
